conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is supported for pharmaceutical-grade oral cannabidiol added to existing antiseizure medicines in children/adolescents with Dravet syndrome, citing randomized controlled trial evidence.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported for *pharmaceutical-grade oral cannabidiol used in addition to existing antiseizure medicines* in children/adolescents with treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome.

The pivotal double-blind randomized trial enrolled 120 patients aged 2–18 years for 14 weeks. Cannabidiol 20 mg/kg/day reduced median convulsive-seizure frequency by 39%, compared with 13% with placebo. A ≥50% reduction occurred in 43% versus 27%, respectively; this responder comparison was not statistically definitive (P=0.08), but the primary seizure-frequency result favored cannabidiol.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28813226/  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618?url_ver=Z39.88-2003&rfr_id=ori:rid:crossref.org&rfr_dat=cr_pub++0pubmed&page=0

A subsequent 199-patient randomized dose-ranging trial replicated the finding: median convulsive-seizure reductions were 48.7% with 10 mg/kg/day and 45.7% with 20 mg/kg/day, versus 26.9% with placebo. The lower dose had a more favorable tolerability profile.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7052786/

Important limits: these trials measured short-term seizure frequency, not cure, developmental outcomes, or long-term effectiveness; results apply to the standardized prescription product, not over-the-counter CBD products. Adverse effects and drug interactions matter—particularly somnolence, reduced appetite, diarrhea, and liver-enzyme elevations (notably with valproate). U.S. labeling indicates cannabidiol for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome in patients aged ≥1 year, with monitoring and dose guidance.  
https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=8bf27097-4870-43fb-94f0-f3d0871d1eec&type=display
